hypothesis: Social traditionalism historically helped Democrats relative to federal baselines.
result_note: Pooled federal-relative association supports traditionalism, but cycle/context adjustment and era-specific estimates are imprecise.

hypothesis: Economic material generosity can coexist with social traditionalism and independently predict overperformance.
result_note: Material generosity is positive only when modeled jointly with social stance; the result disappears with cycle/context controls.

hypothesis: Labor alignment historically helped Democratic candidates.
result_note: Labor has only 17 candidate-cycles and no repeat-candidate coverage.

hypothesis: Punitive law-and-order positioning improves fit in majority-white and federally Republican districts.
result_note: Punitive positioning is associated with presidential-relative performance, not robustly with the combined federal baseline.

hypothesis: Market autonomy improves Democratic fit in conservative districts, separately from material support.

heterogeneity_test: federal R proxy; rural measure pending
result_note: Extraction/property priority has a pooled association, concentrated in 2008-2014 and not robust to cycle/context adjustment.

hypothesis: Issue congruence is more important than a universal moderation score.
result_note: Most majority-white and federal-Republican interaction tests are imprecise; no stable general congruence effect is established.

hypothesis: Ideological advantages attenuate after the 2008 and 2016 nationalization steps.
result_note: The social coefficient is smaller after 2016, but formal attenuation interactions are not statistically distinguishable.

hypothesis: Socially traditional and economically supportive Democrats form the strongest historical bundle.
result_note: Traditional-supportive candidates have the highest raw bundle mean; joint coefficients vanish after cycle/context controls.

hypothesis: The same issue signals predict durable multi-cycle rather than one-cycle overperformance.
result_note: Only 17 repeat people have social scores and only five support a prospective social persistence test.
